questions.prompt: Which four parts does every security policy need?
options: Purpose, scope, roles, enforcement
Title, date, author and page numbers
Tools, budget, vendors, prices
Steps, order, checks, signatures

questions.prompt: In a policy, what does the scope say?
options: Which tool enforces it
Why the policy exists
What happens if it is broken
Who and what it covers

questions.prompt: In a policy, what does the purpose say?
options: Which ports are open
Who must follow it daily
What the steps are
Why the policy exists

questions.prompt: A policy never says what happens if it is broken. What is missing?
options: Scope
Enforcement
Purpose
A password standard

questions.prompt: Why does a policy missing one of its four parts tend to be ignored?
options: The policy becomes too long for anyone to read
Nobody is sure it applies or is enforced
A missing part deletes the policy automatically
Policies with four parts are always too strict

questions.prompt: How detailed is a policy meant to be?
options: Very detailed: every exact step in order
One rule per computer
High-level: the what and the why
A list of passwords to use

questions.prompt: What is a standard?
options: A specific, mandatory rule that supports a policy
A suggestion that can be skipped with good reason
The exact ordered steps for one task
The high-level reason the program exists

questions.prompt: Why do auditors check standards rather than policies?
options: A standard either holds or it doesn't
Policies are kept secret from auditors
Auditors are not allowed to read policies
Standards are always longer than policies

questions.prompt: The standard says passwords need 12+ characters, mixed case, a number and a symbol. Which password complies?
options: ORBIT-RELAY-STATION!
orbitrelaystation7
Orbit-Relay7!kx
Orbit7!

questions.prompt: A password contains the account name. Under the standard, what is true?
options: It is a policy
It does not comply
It is a guideline
It complies if long

questions.prompt: An account breaks the password standard. What should happen?
options: Change the standard to fit it
Note it and check next year
Bring it into compliance now
Delete the whole standard

questions.prompt: What is a procedure?
options: A rule that says "should" not "must"
A recommendation with room for judgment
An exact, ordered sequence of steps
The reason a policy exists at all

questions.prompt: Two people follow the same procedure. What should happen?
options: They skip the steps they think are slow
They do the same thing in the same order
They each choose their own order of steps
They write a new procedure each time

questions.prompt: A tampered log needs restoring from backup. What comes first?
options: Delete the tampered log file
Restore from the latest backup
Email the whole crew about it
Fingerprint the tampered file

questions.prompt: Why does the order of steps matter in a procedure?
options: The computer only accepts steps in one order
Done backwards, they can destroy what you need
Steps run faster in the order they are written
The order never matters if every step is done

questions.prompt: Verify a backup, or delete the original first?
options: Verify the backup first
Do both at the same time
Skip the verification
Delete the original first

questions.prompt: How is a guideline different from a standard?
options: A guideline says "should"; a standard says "must"
A guideline is checked pass or fail by auditors
A guideline says "must"; a standard says "should"
A guideline is the exact steps for a task

questions.prompt: What is a good test for skipping a guideline?
options: Did skipping it save you at least one minute?
Can you explain why this case was different?
Did anyone see you skip the guideline?
Is the guideline more than a year old?

questions.prompt: A guideline says prefer encrypted channels. An urgent shield-failure alert goes over a faster unencrypted channel. Is this right?
options: Yes, if the reason can be explained
Yes, guidelines never matter at all
No, alerts must always be encrypted
No, guidelines can never be skipped

questions.prompt: A routine supply report is sent unencrypted just to save a minute. What is this?
options: Following the standard exactly
Good use of discretion by the whole crew
Skipping the guideline, not judgment
A new procedure for every report

questions.prompt: Why must policies, standards and procedures be reviewed on a schedule?
options: Old documents stop being readable
Auditors require a new font each year
Reviews make the documents shorter
Systems, threats and people change

questions.prompt: Which is a sign a document is stale?
options: It has a clear purpose and a scope
It was reviewed by its owner last month
It has a review date on its first page
It names a system that no longer exists

questions.prompt: What does every document need so it stays current?
options: A longer title and more pages
A copy on every console
An owner and a review date
A password on the file itself

questions.prompt: A procedure was never updated because nobody was assigned to review it. What is the real gap?
options: The procedure had a typo
The procedure was printed
The procedure was too short
No owner and no review date

questions.prompt: A rule has been quietly ignored for months because it no longer fits. What should happen?
options: Punish everyone who ignored it for months
Review it against how work is really done
Keep it exactly as it is and say nothing
Delete every other rule as well

questions.prompt: Which comes last in the top-down flow?
options: Leadership
Standards
Procedures
Policy

questions.prompt: "Protect crew data" is an example of what?
options: A policy
A guideline
A standard
A procedure

questions.prompt: Which word marks a standard?
options: Must
Should
Could
Might

questions.prompt: Which word marks a guideline?
options: Must
Always
Shall
Should

questions.prompt: A document is only reviewed when something breaks. What is wrong?
options: It should never be reviewed at all
It should be reviewed on a schedule
It should be reviewed by the attacker
It should be rewritten every day
